implementation_notes: Togglz is the named Java realization of the whole structure: features are constants of an enum implementing org.togglz.core.Feature, FeatureContext.getFeatureManager().isActive(FEATURE) is the toggle router call, ActivationStrategy implementations (system-properties, user, gradual rollout) are the toggle context, and a StateRepository - FileBasedStateRepository, a database or a cache - owns the state. The JDK alone offers only System.getProperty/getenv, which is why the library-free alternative below exists; without either, Java code tends to grow a Map<String, Boolean> read from everywhere at once.
pitfalls: FeatureContext resolves the FeatureManager through a provider/thread-local: a flag read from a background thread or a different class loader can fail or see a different manager than the request thread.

FileBasedStateRepository rewrites a shared properties file, so two instances or an unlucky redeploy clobber each other's flag state; use a database- or cache-backed repository when more than one node is live.
Domain code that references the feature enum directly re-couples business logic to Togglz; wrap the check behind an injected decision object for library-style code.

variants.name: Constructor-injected Supplier<Boolean> decision object
variants.implementation_notes: Hodgson's third principle in its Java form: the flag is a first-class function - Supplier<Boolean> or a one-method FeatureDecisions interface - injected through the constructor, so the class under test simply receives () -> true or () -> false and never touches System.getProperty, a properties file or a flag library. Reading the configuration and deciding (system property, environment, file, remote store) moves to the wiring layer, which is the only place that knows where the state lives; the heavier Togglz structure above is justified only when flags need an admin console, activation strategies or a persisted state repository.
pitfalls: A Supplier re-reads on every call, which is what a runtime flip needs but also hides the lookup cost in hot loops; hoist it when per-request targeting is not required.
No flag history and no targeting: if the product needs cohorts or an audit trail, the injected function is the wrong level of abstraction.
